description:
Planet X and SPHEREx. We’ll build a public web tool that shows NASA SPHEREx sky images over time and automatically highlights objects that move between images, like asteroids, comets and maybe even new planets. I’ll lead the web app and the data pipeline.

Why join us: we’re focused on building a real working demo, not just slides. That’s what the winning teams in Tashkent did last year. You’ll learn real astronomy data processing, computer vision and web development.
summary:
AralSentinel is a free web tool that helps farmers in Uzbekistan adapt crop rotations to soil salinity and water shortage using NASA Earth observations. More than half of Uzbekistan's irrigated land is affected by salinity, and cotton–wheat monoculture makes it worse, but farmers usually see the damage only when yields fall.

For any field, AralSentinel combines MODIS vegetation (NDVI) and land surface temperature, NASA POWER rainfall and root-zone soil wetness, and SoilGrids soil texture into an explainable salinity-stress risk score. It shows which satellite signal drove the result. A machine-learning trend model forecasts each indicator to 2028. A rotation engine tests 96 three-year rotations (cotton, wheat, sorghum, mung bean, alfalfa, maize) and ranks them by water saving, salt tolerance, soil health and income, weighted by the farmer's own priorities. A simulator estimates yield and income loss if irrigation water is cut.

The tool works in Uzbek, Russian and English, and runs offline. It directly answers the Field Shift challenge: NASA data, local soil information, crop characteristics and farmer priorities combined into practical rotation decisions for one of the world's most salt-affected farming regions.
details:
What it does and how it works

AralSentinel is a web decision-support tool for farmers in salt-affected regions of Uzbekistan. The user picks a field on a satellite map and gets:

1. A salinity-stress risk score (0–100). It combines five inputs: summer land surface temperature (MODIS MOD11A2), vegetation health and its 10-year trend (MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI), root-zone soil wetness and rainfall (NASA POWER), and soil texture and pH (ISRIC SoilGrids). Each input's contribution is shown, so the farmer can see which satellite signal drove the score.

2. A machine-learning trend forecast. A regression model fitted on 2015–2025 NASA data projects each indicator to 2028, with R² shown for transparency.

3. Ranked crop rotations. The engine tests 96 three-year rotations of cotton, winter wheat, sorghum, mung bean, alfalfa and maize. It scores each on water saving, salt tolerance, soil health and estimated income. Sliders let the farmer set priorities, and the ranking updates instantly. Salt tolerance is weighted higher when the field's risk is higher.

4. A water-cut simulator that estimates yield and income loss if irrigation water is cut by 10–50% (FAO-33 yield response method).

Benefits and intended impact

More than half of Uzbekistan's irrigated land is affected by salinity, costing over $1 billion a year, and cotton–wheat monocropping makes it worse. Farmers usually notice damage only when yields fall. AralSentinel shows the risk early and turns it into a practical decision: what to plant next to protect soil and save water. Salt-tolerant crop choices follow ICBA field trials in Uzbekistan. The same method can work in other dry, salt-affected regions in Central Asia, the Middle East and North Africa.

Tools and technologies

Python and FastAPI for data processing and scoring; JavaScript, Leaflet and Chart.js for the web app; NASA POWER API, ORNL DAAC MODIS web service and SoilGrids API for data; Netlify for hosting. The site runs fully from pre-computed data, so it works offline and needs no login.

Creativity

Most rotation tools plan for rainfall. AralSentinel plans for salt, the main threat to farming around the Aral Sea basin. It uses satellite heat stress as a salinity signal, based on research in Syrdarya province showing that canopy temperature tracks soil salinity.

Factors we considered

Farmers' languages (Uzbek, Russian, English), weak internet in rural areas (offline mode), and honesty about limits: satellites do not measure salt directly, so the score is a transparent proxy index, income figures are estimates, and every recommendation advises checking with a local agronomist.
